title: Variation in movements before and after departure from natal territories in a family living bird
content:
Abstract
Species vary in the routes used to obtain breeding vacancies for the first time. In family living species (those that stay with their parents past independence), departing a natal territory in search of a breeding vacancy is predicted to be more costly than staying home. These costs, in combination with the benefits of staying home, predict the occurrence of delayed dispersal. Most research on natal dispersal and routes to breeding has occurred in either cooperatively breeding species or nonsocial species. Here, we examine movements prior to and after departure from natal territories in a family living, non-cooperatively breeding tropical bird, Thamnophilus atrinucha. We found that young individuals engaged in movements away from their natal territory prior to permanent departure, with individuals moving over larger areas and more often as they got older and closer to departure. After permanent departure from their natal territory, individuals initially explored comparatively large areas and then, over time, they settled and traveled within a smaller area. Males explored larger areas than females, suggesting the sexes differ in the costs and benefits of movements or differ in territory acquisition. Due to the challenges of studying young individuals, the behaviors used to find breeding vacancies are poorly understood. Our results indicate this species exhibits exploratory movements both before and after departure and variation in their movements during these two periods may reduce the costs of natal dispersal and increase the probability of territory acquisition.
